title: Equivalent Ratios at the Smoothie Stand
subject: Math
objectives: Students will be able to make equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both quantities by the same number.
Students will be able to find a unit rate and use it to solve a price problem.
standards: CCSS 6.RP.A.3a: make tables of equivalent ratios and plot the pairs on the coordinate plane
materials: A measuring cup (optional, for the warm-up)

vocabulary.meaning: A comparison of two quantities, like 2 cups of mango to 3 cups of yogurt.
Ratios that make the same mix: both parts are multiplied by the same number.
How much for one: the amount per 1 of the other quantity.

sequence.teacher: Show the warm-up. Students answer on whiteboards; ask two students how they got it.
sequence.students: Solve on whiteboards, then hold them up.

slides.title: Warm-up
slides.prompt: Lemonade uses 1 scoop of mix for every 4 cups of water. How much water for 3 scoops?
slides.why: Three scoops is 3 times the mix, so it needs 3 times the water: 3 × 4 = 12.
slides.say: Listen for students who add (1 + 2 = 3, 4 + 2 = 6). That's the mistake today's lesson fixes.

sequence.teacher: Teach equivalent ratios with the tape diagram, show a ratio on a graph, then model a unit price problem.

slides.say: Read each word aloud and have students repeat it.

slides.title: A ratio is a recipe
points: 2 cups mango for every 3 cups yogurt: **2 : 3**

diagram.description: Tape diagram: 2 mango boxes above 3 yogurt boxes, equal-size boxes.

slides.callout: **Multiply both parts by the same number.** Adding the same amount changes the taste.
slides.say: Point to each box: one box is one cup. A double batch draws every box twice.

slides.title: Is 4 : 6 the same mix as 2 : 3?
slides.problem: Mia uses 4 cups of mango and 6 cups of yogurt. Does her smoothie taste the same as 2 : 3?
steps: Find what 2 was multiplied by to get 4: **× 2**.
Multiply the 3 by the same number: 3 × 2 = **6**.
Mia's 6 cups of yogurt matches, so the ratios are equivalent.
slides.say: Pause before each step and ask the class what comes next.

slides.title: Ratios on a graph
points: Each table row is a point: (scoops, cups)

diagram.description: A grid, scoops 0-5 across and cups 0-10 up, with points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) joined by a line from (0, 0).

slides.say: Lemonade: 1 scoop makes 2 cups. Plot (1, 2) together: across 1, up 2. Have students say where (2, 4) goes before you point.

slides.title: How much for one?
slides.problem: 4 juice boxes cost $6. How much does 1 juice box cost?
steps: One box is a quarter of 4 boxes, so divide both by 4.
slides.answer: $1.50 per juice box. That's the unit rate.
slides.say: Connect to the warm-up: dividing both parts keeps the ratio the same, just like multiplying.

slides.title: Multiply, don't add
slides.callout: Turn and talk: why does adding change the taste?
slides.say: Give 1 minute to talk. Listen for: adding gives the yogurt fewer extra cups than it needs.

sequence.teacher: One item for each kind of worksheet question. Whiteboards; reveal after everyone shows.

slides.title: We do: fill the table
slides.prompt: Paint: 3 cans of blue for every 1 can of white. How many cans of blue for 4 cans of white?
slides.why: 4 cans of white is 4 times the recipe, so 3 × 4 = 12 cans of blue.
slides.say: This is the worksheet's table move: multiply both parts by the same number.

slides.title: We do: how much for one?
slides.prompt: 5 notebooks cost $10. How much does 1 notebook cost?
slides.why: Divide the cost by the number of notebooks: $10 ÷ 5 = $2.
slides.say: Ask: which number goes first? Dollars ÷ items gives dollars for one item.

slides.title: We do: same ratio?
slides.prompt: Which ratio makes the same mix as 3 : 5?
slides.why: 3 : 5 times 2 is 6 : 10. The others add, or multiply only one part.
slides.say: Ask a student who picked A to explain, then show why it doesn't work.

sequence.then: Finished early? On the back, write your own smoothie recipe and two batches that taste the same.
sequence.teacher: Circulate. For students stuck on Q1, point to the 1-batch row and ask what changed. Collect every sheet when time's up.
sequence.students: Complete the worksheet on their own.

sequence.teacher: Students answer on a sticky note and stick it on the door on the way out.
sequence.students: Answer on a sticky note, on their own.

slides.title: Exit ticket
slides.prompt: On a sticky note: 8 pencils cost $4. What does 1 pencil cost? Show how you know.
slides.say: Sort the sticky notes: right, set up but wrong, and not started. That's tomorrow's grouping.

checks: What did we multiply by to get from 2 : 3 to 6 : 9?
What does "per" mean in a unit rate?

misconceptions.misconception: Adding the same number to both parts keeps the ratio (2 : 3 → 4 : 5).
misconceptions.response: Draw the tape diagram for both and compare: the yogurt boxes don't match.

misconceptions.misconception: Dividing the number of items by the cost (6 ÷ 15) when the question asks for the cost of one.
misconceptions.response: Ask: what are we finding one of? Put the dollars first: dollars ÷ items gives dollars for one item.

support: Give a ratio table with the 1-batch row filled in.
Let students use the tape diagram on the worksheet.
extension: Find the unit rate for yogurt per cup of mango (1.5).
Write a ratio that is NOT equivalent and explain why.
language: Post the sentence frame: "For every __ cups of mango, there are __ cups of yogurt."
Say ratio and razón (Spanish) together when you show the vocabulary slide.

homework: Find a recipe at home and write it as a ratio. Then write a double batch.

walkthrough.think: What happens to the mango and yogurt from 1 batch to 2 batches?
walkthrough.idea: Every row multiplies both parts of 2 : 3 by the number of batches.
mistakes: Adding 2 to each row instead of multiplying.

walkthrough.think: What do you divide to find the cost of one?
walkthrough.idea: Divide the cost by the number of smoothies.
mistakes: Dividing 6 by 15: that's smoothies per dollar, not dollars per smoothie.

walkthrough.think: Which number in each pair goes across, and which goes up?
walkthrough.idea: Each table row is a point: mango across, yogurt up.
steps: Start at 0, go across 2 and up 3. Dot.
Connect with a ruler: equivalent ratios make a straight line.

walkthrough.think: Can you get from 2 : 3 to the choice by multiplying both parts by one number?
steps: A, C, and D can't be made by multiplying both parts by the same number.
mistakes: Picking C, which adds 2 to each part.

assessment: A student who has it fills a ratio table by multiplying both parts, finds a unit price by dividing the cost by the number of items, and can say why adding the same amount to both parts changes the ratio.
